selection_policy: Include a legal benchmark or adjacent evaluation resource only when an official or primary source defines its task and scoring contract. Separate fixed benchmarks from datasets, frameworks, annual shared tasks, private tests, and resource lists; record access limits and unresolved claims instead of filling gaps by inference.

entries.name: LegalBench
entries.capability: Task-specific legal reasoning across classification, extraction, question answering, and generation.
entries.construct: The suite operationalizes six lawyer-facing forms of legal reasoning through 162 independently authored tasks; it is a task collection, not a single latent legal-intelligence score.

data.size: 162 tasks; per-task instance counts vary
data.source: Expert-contributed tasks plus public legal datasets and authorities
data.input: Prompt plus task-specific facts, rules, clauses, or questions
data.output: Labels, spans, short answers, or generated text depending on task

metrics.name: Task-defined exact match / accuracy / F1 / generation scores
metrics.protocol: Each task supplies its own scorer; aggregate results must disclose task selection and averaging.

entries.baselines: Paper evaluates 20 open and commercial LLMs; external Vals results are not the canonical paper leaderboard.

access.license: Repository/data licenses vary by contributed task

entries.maintenance: Active collaborative repository; pin a commit because tasks and harness behavior can change.
entries.reproducibility: Code, prompts, and public labels are available; cross-paper comparison requires the same task subset, prompt protocol, and model version.
risks: Public prompts and gold labels create direct contamination and overfitting risk.
Averaging heterogeneous tasks can hide severe failures in legally important sub-capabilities.

verified: Official paper and repository identify 162 tasks and six reasoning categories.
inference: The suite is best used diagnostically rather than as a single legal-intelligence rank.
ambiguities: Constituent task licenses are not uniform.

entries.name: LexEval
entries.capability: Chinese legal knowledge, inference, generation, discrimination, and ethics across 23 tasks.
entries.construct: Six ability groups broaden evaluation beyond exams, but accuracy and ROUGE-L remain task proxies rather than a validated unidimensional legal-capability scale.

data.size: 14,150 questions across 23 tasks and six ability groups
data.splits: Evaluation collection; mostly multiple choice plus generation
data.source: Chinese legal exams, public datasets, authored and transformed tasks
data.input: Questions, facts, choices, or generation prompts

metrics.name: Accuracy
metrics.protocol: Exact option/label correctness for closed-form tasks.

metrics.name: ROUGE-L
metrics.protocol: Longest-common-subsequence overlap for generated answers.

entries.baselines: Official paper evaluates general and legal-domain LLMs; the historical Collam site is not a stable leaderboard.
entries.maintenance: Research release; claims of continuous updating are not a substitute for semantic versions.
entries.reproducibility: Public prompts and data support reruns; pin task revision and generation decoding.
risks: Public exams and answers are highly contamination-prone.
ROUGE-L can reward surface overlap without legal validity.

verified: Official repository and paper define 14,150 questions and 23 tasks.
ambiguities: No stable current official leaderboard or project page was verified; the historical Collam hostname currently fails TLS validation.

entries.name: ArabLegalEval
entries.capability: Arabic legal knowledge, classification, question answering, and translation, with substantial Saudi-law coverage.
entries.construct: The suite combines local and translated tasks; task scores therefore mix Arabic legal competence, general task performance, and translation artifacts.

data.size: HF card exposes about 15.3k ArLegalBench rows, 11.6k MCQs, and 79 QA rows
data.source: Local legal material, translated benchmarks, and synthetic items
data.input: Arabic questions, text, choices, or translation prompts

metrics.name: Accuracy / F1 / ROUGE
metrics.protocol: Task-specific closed-form and overlap metrics.

metrics.name: LLM and human ratings
metrics.protocol: GPT-4-style judge scores for some generation plus human translation ratings; record the exact judge prompt/model.

entries.baselines: Paper evaluates Arabic-capable and frontier LLMs across configurations.

access.license: No single clear unified code/data license located

entries.maintenance: HF and GitHub artifacts exist; pin revision because configurations have evolved.
entries.reproducibility: Mixed: public data, but judge/model versions and configuration counts require careful pinning.
risks: Synthetic GPT-4/Claude items and translated tasks can introduce generator artifacts.
The QA component is very small relative to the multiple-choice collection.

verified: Official organization GitHub/HF and paper establish the suite identity.
ambiguities: A unified release-wide license was not found.

entries.name: ALARB
entries.capability: Reason over Saudi commercial-law cases, complete arguments, and identify governing statutory articles.
entries.construct: Verdict/argument generation is judged for correctness and partial correctness, while article selection uses MCQ accuracy; the protocol mixes open and closed-form constructs.

data.size: 13,344 cases linked to eight statutes; reported experiments use 1,329 cases and 1,159 MCQs per article task
data.splits: HF exposes a release without a clearly isolated hidden test
data.source: Saudi commercial cases and statutes, restructured with LLM assistance
data.input: Case facts/reasoning context or article question

metrics.name: Correct / partial / incorrect judge score
metrics.protocol: GPT-4o categorizes generated legal outputs against references.

metrics.name: MCQ accuracy
metrics.protocol: Exact statutory-article choice.

entries.baselines: Paper evaluates multiple Arabic/general LLMs.
entries.maintenance: Fixed research release; no canonical GitHub repository located.
entries.reproducibility: Data are inspectable, but hosted-judge drift and absence of a hidden split limit strict reproduction.
risks: LLM-assisted restructuring and mapping can propagate annotation errors.
Public cases, labels, and references permit contamination and evaluation-set training.

verified: Paper and THIQAH-RD HF release identify the dataset.
ambiguities: No canonical GitHub or independent leaderboard was found.

entries.name: ContractEval
entries.capability: Evaluate long-context LLM clause-risk extraction on the public CUAD test set.
entries.construct: F1/F2 and Jaccard trade off overlap precision and recall, while false-no-related-clause rate isolates abstention failures; the protocol reuses CUAD rather than defining new ground truth.

data.size: CUAD test set, about 4,182 QA rows over 41 categories
data.source: CUAD
data.input: Contract plus clause question

metrics.name: F1 / F2 / Jaccard
metrics.protocol: Overlap scores; F2 weights recall twice as strongly as precision.

metrics.name: False no-related-clause rate
metrics.protocol: Share of positive items incorrectly rejected as containing no relevant clause.

entries.baselines: Paper evaluates 19 contemporary LLMs under one protocol.

access.license: No separate dataset; CUAD terms apply

entries.maintenance: Paper protocol, not a separately maintained benchmark release.
entries.reproducibility: Moderate if prompts/model versions are available; public API aliases can drift.
risks: It is not a new dataset and should not be counted as independent evidence from CUAD.
Paper figures use both 4,128 and 4,182, an unresolved count inconsistency.

verified: The protocol evaluates CUAD rather than releasing new labeled examples.
ambiguities: 4,128 versus 4,182 evaluation rows.

entries.name: MSLR-Bench
entries.capability: Extract structured facts and produce IRAC-style reasoning for Chinese insider-trading cases.
entries.construct: Field-level extraction metrics test factual structure; IRAC recall and an LLM judge test whether generated analysis covers expected legal reasoning components.

data.size: 1,389 cases from 2005–2024 with 59,771 fields
data.splits: HF visibly exposes one train split
data.source: Public Chinese insider-trading enforcement/case materials
data.input: Case documents
data.output: Structured JSON fields and free-text IRAC analysis

metrics.name: Field accuracy / FCR
metrics.protocol: Exact or normalized field correctness plus the paper's field-completion/consistency measure.

metrics.name: IRAC Recall and judge score
metrics.protocol: Recall of expected IRAC elements plus LLM evaluation of generated reasoning.

entries.baselines: Official paper compares general and legal LLMs; headline percentages must be tied to a named metric.

access.license: GitHub Apache-2.0 versus HF MIT metadata conflict

entries.reproducibility: Public artifacts exist, but split isolation, license metadata, and judge version require resolution.
risks: One visible split allows accidental train/evaluation overlap.
Public cases and a single LLM judge create contamination and evaluator-bias risk.

verified: Official GitHub/HF/paper agree on the case/field scale.
ambiguities: Repository and HF licenses conflict; no hidden held-out split was verified.

entries.name: MASLegalBench
entries.capability: Multi-agent deductive reasoning about GDPR enforcement facts, rules, application, common sense, and conclusions.
entries.construct: Accuracy measures final MCQ correctness; retrieval-at-k tests evidence acquisition; refusal and agreement statistics diagnose coordination rather than legal validity directly.

data.size: 950 MCQs from 15 UK enforcement reports: 647 yes/no and 303 four-choice
data.source: Fifteen UK regulatory enforcement reports; questions generated with DeepSeek and reviewed
data.input: Question plus retrievable report chunks

metrics.name: Accuracy / refusal rate
metrics.protocol: Exact final answer correctness and share of non-answers.

metrics.name: Retrieval@1/3/5 and Cohen's kappa
metrics.protocol: Evidence-hit rates plus agent/human agreement statistics.

entries.baselines: Paper compares single- and multi-agent configurations.
entries.reproducibility: Prompts/code are public; hosted models and multi-agent stochasticity need repeated trials.
risks: Only 15 source reports sharply limit source diversity.
Generator-authored questions can encode DeepSeek artifacts and source overlap.

verified: Official paper/repository define 950 questions and the 647/303 split.

entries.name: LegalEval-Q
entries.capability: Predict the quality of Chinese LLM-generated legal answers.
entries.construct: A learned five-dimension regressor and adjusted aggregate score approximate human quality labels; it evaluates outputs, not legal tasks against authoritative answers.

data.size: About 10k source queries; 946 annotated items, about 9,460 model-output annotations, and 60 validation items
data.source: Legal queries, model responses, and AI-assisted/human quality annotations
data.input: Question and generated legal answer
data.output: Five dimension scores and adjusted aggregate

metrics.name: Dimension regression / AdjScore
metrics.protocol: Predict per-dimension quality labels and combine them with the paper's adjustment formula.

entries.baselines: Paper compares evaluator models and correlation/agreement with annotations.

access.gating: Some model artifacts may require external platform access

entries.reproducibility: Limited by licensing, model artifacts, and the small validation set.
risks: Training an evaluator on AI-assisted annotations can create circular model-family bias.
A high evaluator score is not independent proof that an answer is legally correct.

verified: Official paper/repository define it as an answer-quality evaluator.
ambiguities: Public license and complete artifact accessibility remain unresolved.

entries.name: LRAGE
entries.capability: Configure legal RAG evaluations across retrievers, rerankers, agents, judges, and custom corpora.
entries.construct: LRAGE supplies orchestration rather than one fixed construct; validity is inherited from the selected corpus, task, judge, and metric configuration.

data.size: No fixed dataset
data.splits: Uses LegalBench, LawBench, KBL, Pile-of-Law, PLAT, bar-exam QA, housing QA, or custom JSON
data.source: User-selected public/custom corpora
data.input: Configured corpus, queries, and pipeline
data.output: Retrieval, reranking, answer, and optional judge results

metrics.name: Inherited task/retrieval/judge metrics
metrics.protocol: Metric set is configuration-dependent and must be reported with corpus and judge versions.

entries.baselines: Paper demonstrates multiple legal RAG configurations; there is no one unified leaderboard.

access.license: MIT framework; selected corpus licenses vary

entries.reproducibility: Potentially strong with a frozen config and dependencies; weak when users omit judge/model/corpus revisions.
risks: Cross-run comparisons are invalid when configurations differ.
It inherits every selected corpus's leakage, rights, and temporal-validity risks.

verified: Official paper/repository describe a configurable framework rather than a fixed benchmark.

entries.name: prinzbench
entries.capability: Answer obscure US legal-research and general information-search questions.
entries.construct: Single-author human pass/fail attempts to measure research usefulness, but withheld items and non-blind grading prevent independent construct validation.

data.size: 33 withheld questions: 25 legal research and 8 search; three runs each (99 evaluations)
data.source: Author-created withheld questions
data.input: Free-form research question

metrics.name: Human pass/fail and pass@1
metrics.protocol: Author judges each answer; subtotals by legal/search category.

entries.baselines: Repository reports selected model results; outsiders cannot rerun the same questions.
entries.reproducibility: Not independently reproducible.
risks: Hidden questions reduce contamination but also block auditability and independent scoring.
Single-author non-blind judgments may reflect unmeasured preferences.

verified: Public repository describes 33 private questions and 99 runs.
ambiguities: Question contents, rubric detail, and license are unavailable.

entries.name: Open Legal-Answer Benchmark
entries.capability: Produce current US legal answers with relevant, supported, and correctly ranged citations.
entries.construct: Checklist and citation metrics separate substantive required points, forbidden claims, authority retrieval, and citation entailment/range instead of collapsing answer quality into one judge score.

data.size: 54 base questions (29 hard, 25 controls) plus 8 adversarial variants; 62 JSONL rows
data.source: Sponsor-authored current-law questions and cited authorities
data.input: Legal question

metrics.name: Must-include / must-not / authority retrieval
metrics.protocol: Rule/checklist scoring of required propositions, prohibited errors, and retrieval of the right authority.

metrics.name: Citation support and in-range
metrics.protocol: Check whether citations support the associated claim and point to the relevant passage; optional LLM judging is separate.

entries.baselines: Sponsor-maintained self-runs are recorded in the repository leaderboard.
entries.maintenance: Active sponsor-maintained benchmark; versioning matters for current-law questions.
entries.reproducibility: Public data and scorer support reruns; browser/search availability and current sources can change outcomes.
risks: Fully public questions permit direct optimization.
Sponsor-run results are not an independent third-party audit.

verified: Official repository exposes the 62-row JSONL and leaderboard.
ambiguities: Temporal legal changes can make older gold expectations stale.

entries.name: LawBench
entries.capability: Chinese legal memorization, understanding, and application across 20 tasks.
entries.construct: Tasks are arranged into memorization, understanding, and application levels, testing retrieval of legal knowledge separately from applying it to cases and generated outputs.

data.size: 10,000 examples: 20 tasks × 500
data.splits: Evaluation-oriented task files; no unified hidden split
data.source: Chinese exams and public legal NLP datasets including CAIL/JEC-QA/LAIC sources
data.input: Task-specific JSON text, questions, facts, or documents
data.output: Choices, labels, extracted items, numeric values, or generated text

metrics.name: Official 20-task metric map
metrics.protocol: 1-1 ROUGE-L; 1-2 accuracy; 2-1 F0.5; 2-2 F1; 2-3 F1; 2-4 accuracy; 2-5 character-level rc-F1; 2-6 entity soft-F1; 2-7 ROUGE-L; 2-8 accuracy; 2-9 F1; 2-10 trigger soft-F1; 3-1 F1; 3-2 ROUGE-L; 3-3 F1; 3-4 and 3-5 normalized log-distance; 3-6 accuracy; 3-7 accuracy; 3-8 ROUGE-L. Report per-task scores because the official AVG mixes unlike scales.

metrics.name: Normalized log-distance (3-4/3-5)
metrics.protocol: For scorable prison-term items, score = 1 - mean(|ln(gold_months+1)-ln(pred_months+1)|)/ln(216). The evaluator uses the first parsed month value, otherwise the first year value multiplied by 12; an unparsed prediction receives distance ln(216). Gold death/life-imprisonment rows are skipped.

metrics.name: Abstention rate
metrics.protocol: The evaluator separately reports the fraction of rows whose answer parser cannot extract a valid task-specific response. This is not folded consistently into every task score, and the 2-6 evaluator misspells its returned abstention key, so the top-level CSV records zero for that task unless corrected.

entries.baselines: Official paper compares general and legal-domain LLMs; OpenCompass hosts results.

access.dataset: Public GitHub release; linked HF copy is third-party
access.license: Repository license applies to code; source-dataset terms vary

entries.maintenance: Repository is available; use a pinned revision.
entries.reproducibility: Prompts and evaluator code are public, but there is no canonical author-owned HF dataset and source tasks have mixed provenance. Pin and inspect the scorer: parsing rules, skipped rows, and abstention handling affect the result.
risks: Public exam and CAIL-derived answers create high contamination risk.
The headline AVG arithmetically mixes heterogeneous task metrics, while task-specific parsers and inconsistent abstention handling can change scores.
A third-party HF mirror can drift from the canonical repository.

verified: Official repository defines 20 tasks with 500 samples per task.
Official README and evaluator code define the task-to-metric map, normalized log-distance, and parser-based abstention reporting.
inference: Per-task reporting is more interpretable than the heterogeneous official AVG.
ambiguities: No official canonical HF release was located.
The official 2-6 evaluator returns the misspelled key 'anstention_rate', so the top-level evaluator silently writes zero abstention for that task.

entries.name: Massive Legal Embedding Benchmark
entries.capability: Legal embedding quality across retrieval, retrieval-augmented QA, and zero-shot classification tasks.
entries.construct: MTEB-compatible task configurations treat rank quality—usually nDCG@10—as the main proxy for useful legal representations, supplemented by QA and classification task scores.

data.size: 10 constituent datasets
data.source: Public legal retrieval, QA, and classification datasets assembled by Isaacus
data.input: Queries and candidate texts or labeled examples
data.output: Ranked candidates, answers, or zero-shot labels

metrics.name: nDCG@10
metrics.protocol: Discounted graded gain at rank 10, normalized by the ideal ranking; constituent tasks may add QA/classification metrics.

entries.baselines: Public result files and an Isaacus-hosted leaderboard compare general and legal embedding models.

access.license: MIT code; constituent dataset licenses vary

entries.maintenance: Active vendor-maintained suite; pin task configs and result commit.
entries.reproducibility: Evaluator is public and MTEB-compatible; API embeddings and changing hosted model aliases can still move scores.
risks: All public queries and labels permit benchmark-targeted optimization.
Benchmark owner also sells a leading model, so independently reproduced results are preferable.

verified: Both source README bullets resolve to the same GitHub repository and benchmark identity.
ambiguities: The original awesome-list Kanon/MLEB URL could not be verified as canonical.

entries.name: Contract Understanding Atticus Dataset
entries.capability: Locate 41 categories of commercially important clauses in long contracts.
entries.construct: Extractive QA turns issue spotting into span retrieval: a model should find every relevant token while avoiding unrelated language and correctly abstain when a clause is absent.

data.size: 510 contracts; 13,000+ expert labels; common QA release has 22,450 train and 4,182 test rows
data.source: Material contracts filed in SEC EDGAR
data.input: Contract text plus a clause-category question
data.output: One or more answer spans, or no answer

metrics.name: Token intersection-over-union (Jaccard)
metrics.protocol: |predicted-token set ∩ gold-token set| / |union|, with precision/recall and AUPR across confidence thresholds.

metrics.name: AUPR
metrics.protocol: Area under the precision–recall curve over clause predictions, useful under strong class imbalance.

entries.baselines: Paper reports BERT-family extractive QA baselines; many later long-context systems reuse the public test set.

access.license: CC BY 4.0 for annotations/release; source contracts retain underlying rights

entries.reproducibility: Data and evaluation code are public; normalize tokenization and no-answer handling exactly.
risks: Public contracts and gold spans are heavily reused and contamination-prone.
Boilerplate similarity can reward memorization more than issue spotting on novel drafting styles.

verified: Official project, GitHub, paper, and author HF release agree on the benchmark identity.
ambiguities: Published descriptions count annotations, QA rows, and labels differently; state which unit is reported.

entries.name: LEDGAR
entries.capability: Classify contract provisions into clause/topic labels.
entries.construct: Provision classification measures whether representations separate contract-language topics; macro-F1 exposes rare-label performance while micro-F1 emphasizes the frequent-label mass.

data.size: Original corpus: about 846,274 provisions, 12,608 labels, 60,540 contracts; LexGLUE subset: 60k/10k/10k over 100 labels
data.source: SEC EDGAR contracts
data.input: A contract provision

metrics.name: Micro-F1 and macro-F1
metrics.protocol: Micro pools all label decisions; macro averages per-label F1 so rare labels have equal weight.

entries.baselines: Original paper and LexGLUE report neural and transformer classifiers.

access.dataset: Public code/data paths; LexGLUE package is directly loadable
access.license: LexGLUE package CC BY 4.0; underlying filing rights and original release terms should be reviewed

entries.maintenance: Original dataset is stable; LexGLUE is the maintained standardized task.
entries.reproducibility: Strong if the exact original versus LexGLUE variant, label vocabulary, and split are named.
risks: SEC boilerplate enables document-family leakage and near-duplicate memorization.
Reporting LEDGAR without naming the original or 100-label LexGLUE variant is ambiguous.

verified: The README's Metatext link is secondary; the original repository and LexGLUE are canonical sources.
ambiguities: Source-rights treatment is not identical to the annotation license.

entries.name: ECtHR Tasks A/B
entries.capability: Predict European Convention articles alleged (Task A) or found violated (Task B) from case facts.
entries.construct: Multi-label outcome prediction tests fact-to-doctrine mapping; macro-F1 emphasizes less frequent Convention articles and micro-F1 the total decision mass.
jurisdictions: European Court of Human Rights / Council of Europe

data.size: Roughly 11,000 cases per LexGLUE Task A/B configuration
data.source: Public ECtHR judgments and case facts
data.input: Case-fact section

metrics.name: Micro-F1 and macro-F1
metrics.protocol: F1 is computed over article labels with micro and label-macro aggregation.

entries.baselines: Original Chalkidis et al. work and LexGLUE report transformer and long-document baselines.

access.dataset: Public LexGLUE configs ecthr_a and ecthr_b

entries.maintenance: Stable LexGLUE release; the older coastalcph/ecthr_cases HF path is stale.
entries.reproducibility: Good with the exact task config, long-document truncation strategy, and thresholding specified.
risks: Judgments and labels are public and likely represented in pretraining corpora.
Outcome labels can be learned from stylistic or temporal shortcuts rather than legal reasoning.

verified: LexGLUE is the current canonical distribution path.
ambiguities: Counts vary slightly across original and standardized releases.

entries.name: awesome-legal-nlp
entries.capability: Discovery index for legal NLP datasets, models, papers, surveys, books, and events.
entries.construct: No evaluation construct is defined; this is a curated bibliography/resource list, not an instrument for measuring model capability.

data.size: No benchmark instances
data.source: Community-curated links
data.input: Not applicable

metrics.name: Not applicable
metrics.protocol: No scorer or evaluation protocol exists.

entries.baselines: None.
entries.reproducibility: Not applicable as an evaluation artifact.
risks: Treating a resource list as a benchmark confuses discovery coverage with measured capability.

verified: Repository contents are links and prose rather than instances, gold labels, or graders.

entries.name: JUST-NLP 2025 Legal MT Shared Task
entries.capability: Translate legal text from English to Hindi.
entries.construct: Reference-based machine-translation metrics reward n-gram or character overlap; the shared task complements them with semantic metrics but still cannot alone establish legal fidelity.

data.size: InLMT: 50,000 train, 5,000 validation, 5,000 hidden test sentences
data.splits: Train/validation plus hidden Codabench test references
data.source: Indian legal parallel text released for the shared task
data.input: XLSX rows containing English legal sentences and IDs
data.output: CSV with ID and Hindi translation

metrics.name: AutoRank
metrics.protocol: Arithmetic mean of six 0–100 normalized metrics: BLEU, METEOR, inverted TER, chrF++, BERTScore, and COMET; each receives equal weight.

metrics.name: BLEU / METEOR / TER / chrF++ / BERTScore / COMET
metrics.protocol: Report all six component metrics; higher is better except raw TER, where lower is better. ROUGE scores appear in additional model analysis but are not part of AutoRank.

entries.baselines: The findings paper's Table 2 ranks Team-SVNIT first at AutoRank 61.62; the abstract instead says the highest AutoRank was 72.1, an unresolved internal conflict.

access.license: Not clearly stated in the durable public materials
access.gating: Codabench account may be required for files/submission

entries.maintenance: Completed 2025 shared task; not a continuously maintained benchmark.
entries.reproducibility: Hidden references support clean competition scoring, but long-term artifact access and exact dependency versions are uncertain.
risks: Automatic overlap metrics can reward fluent mistranslations or penalize legally equivalent wording.
The original README linked stale Codabench competition 3682; 10351 is the verified competition.

verified: The official findings paper and competition materials define the 50k/5k/5k splits, six AutoRank components, normalization direction, and equal-weight aggregation.
ambiguities: A clear dataset license was not located.
The findings abstract reports a top AutoRank of 72.1 while Table 2 and the official result sheet report 61.62.

entries.name: LegalBench-RAG
entries.capability: Retrieve exact supporting spans from long legal and policy documents.
entries.construct: Character-level precision and recall directly measure whether retrieved text covers gold support while limiting extra context; this isolates retrieval from answer generation.

data.size: 714 documents, more than 79M characters; 6,858 queries in abstract versus 6,889 in a paper table
data.source: Four public contract/policy datasets
data.input: Query plus document corpus
data.output: Document identifier and character start/end spans

metrics.name: Character precision and recall
metrics.protocol: Overlap between predicted and reference character sets, exposing both missed support and context bloat.

entries.baselines: Paper evaluates retrieval systems at several context budgets.

access.license: MIT code; constituent source licenses vary

entries.reproducibility: High for retrieval when the exact commit, corpus, character normalization, and context budget are pinned.
risks: No hidden split; queries, corpus, and spans are public.
The paper's query counts conflict and should never be silently harmonized.

verified: Official repository and paper define exact-span evaluation.
ambiguities: 6,858 versus 6,889 query count remains unresolved.

entries.name: LegalAgentBench
entries.capability: Chinese legal tool use, multi-hop information gathering, and legal writing.
entries.construct: Success and progress scores estimate whether an agent selects and sequences tools toward a task; BERTScore assesses writing similarity, but neither alone proves legal correctness.

data.size: 17 corpora, 37 tools, 300 tasks
data.splits: Tasks span one-to-five-hop and writing categories
data.source: Chinese legal corpora wrapped as tools and authored tasks
data.input: Natural-language task plus tool environment
data.output: JSON tool calls and a final legal answer or document

metrics.name: Keyword success rate / progress rate
metrics.protocol: Rule-based matching of required milestones and final keywords across task trajectories.

metrics.name: BERTScore
metrics.protocol: Contextual token similarity for generated legal writing; token use is also reported.

entries.baselines: Paper compares multiple LLM agents and prompting configurations.

access.dataset: Public code, data, prompts, and environment
access.gating: Model/API credentials may be needed to run baselines

entries.reproducibility: Harness is public; API model drift and environment dependencies still affect trajectories.
risks: Keyword graders can be gamed without producing a legally adequate result.
Public solutions and tool corpora permit benchmark-specific planning.

verified: Official repository specifies 17 corpora, 37 tools, and 300 tasks.
inference: Use as a tool-use benchmark with legal grounding checks, not as proof of deployable lawyering.

entries.name: LEXam
entries.capability: Answer bilingual law-school multiple-choice and open-answer examination questions.
entries.construct: MCQ accuracy measures answer selection; open-answer ensemble judging estimates substantive coverage against references, making judge version and rubric part of the instrument.

data.size: 7,537 questions from 340 exams and 116 courses: 2,841 open-answer and 4,696 MCQ
data.splits: Versioned JSON release; no single training split is required
data.source: University law examinations and course materials
data.input: Question, optional choices, and metadata

metrics.name: MCQ accuracy
metrics.protocol: Exact selected-option correctness.

metrics.name: Open-answer judge ensemble
metrics.protocol: Multiple LLM judges score generated answers against references; record judge model versions and aggregation.

entries.baselines: Official results compare broad frontier/open models; project site tracks benchmark resources.
entries.maintenance: Active versioned benchmark; item count changed from an earlier 4,886-item release.
entries.reproducibility: Good when dataset revision, prompts, judge ensemble, and model endpoints are pinned.
risks: Public exams and answers are contamination-prone.
Open-answer rankings can move when hosted judges or ensemble membership changes.

verified: Official GitHub/HF/project sources agree on the current 7,537-question release.
ambiguities: Jurisdiction is course-dependent rather than a single national-law corpus.

entries.name: LexGLUE
entries.capability: Standardized English legal language understanding across seven classification and judgment tasks.
entries.construct: LexGLUE standardizes task splits and reporting across ECtHR A/B, SCOTUS, EUR-LEX, LEDGAR, UNFAIR-ToS, and CaseHOLD; it measures a portfolio of NLU tasks rather than one jurisdiction-neutral ability.

data.size: Seven constituent datasets
data.source: Previously released legal datasets normalized by the LexGLUE authors
data.input: Case facts, opinions, provisions, legislation, or terms of service

metrics.name: Macro-F1 and micro-F1 / task accuracy
metrics.protocol: Task-appropriate classification metrics; report each task and disclose any cross-task averaging.

entries.baselines: Official repository reports BERT, RoBERTa, LegalBERT, hierarchical, Longformer, and BigBird baselines.

access.license: CC BY 4.0 package; constituent-source rights should still be checked

entries.reproducibility: High when task config, long-document handling, thresholds, and aggregate convention are pinned.
risks: All constituent test labels are public and likely present in model-development workflows.
A single aggregate hides jurisdiction and task-family failures.

verified: Official GitHub/HF/paper define seven tasks and standardized splits.
inference: LexGLUE is a strong comparability suite, not a deployability claim.

entries.name: Competition on Legal Information Extraction/Entailment
entries.capability: Retrieve and recognize entailment among Canadian cases and Japanese civil-code provisions.
entries.construct: Four annual tasks separate first-stage authority retrieval from textual entailment; official hidden tests reduce direct leakage, while task-specific precision/recall/F1 and accuracy measure different stages.

data.size: Annual task packages; counts change by year
data.splits: Released training data plus competition-held test labels
data.source: Canadian case law and Japanese civil-code/bar-exam materials

entries.name: LeCaRDv2
entries.capability: Retrieve legally similar Chinese criminal cases using graded relevance across characterization, penalty, and procedure.
entries.construct: Expert multi-aspect relevance separates factual/legal similarity from mere lexical overlap; recall at large k tests first-stage retrieval and nDCG/precision support reranking analysis.

data.size: 800 query cases, 55,192 judged candidates sampled from 4.3M criminal cases
data.splits: 640 train / 160 test queries for the reported fine-tuning setup
data.source: Chinese criminal judgments with expert graded relevance
data.input: Query case and candidate case corpus

metrics.name: Recall@100/200/500/1000
metrics.protocol: Coverage of judged relevant cases at first-stage retrieval cutoffs.

metrics.name: nDCG / precision at k
metrics.protocol: Graded ranking quality and top-result relevance for reranking settings.

entries.baselines: Official paper/repository compare sparse, dense, and legal-pretrained retrieval/reranking methods.
entries.reproducibility: Good with the official candidate pool and qrels; full 4.3M source corpus handling may vary.
risks: Judged candidate pooling can miss relevant cases outside the pool.
Chronological and court-source shortcuts may inflate similarity.

verified: Official repository/paper establish 800 queries, 55,192 candidates, and 4.3M source cases.
